newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle crew set for Hubble tune-up. [CORRECTED 19:55 GMT]
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle crew set for Hubble tune-up. [CORRECTED 19:55 GMT]

text.p: The crew of the shuttle Discovery on Wednesday flexed the spacecraft's robot arm, checked their spacesuits and said they were ready for a $350 million (corrects to insert dropped word "million") service call on the orbiting Hubble telescope.
Discovery trailed Hubble by 574 miles (924 km) on Wednesday morning and was closing in on the telescope by about 70 miles (113 km) with each orbit of the earth.
Final preparations were under way to retrieve the telescope early on Thursday morning and start a four-day series of spacewalks to refurbish the telescope and vastly improve it.

NASA astronaut Steve Hawley, who used the shuttle's robot arm in 1990 to gently lift the telescope into orbit, put the Canadian-built arm through its paces late on Tuesday to make sure it was working properly.
Hawley will reach out with the 50-foot (15 metre) arm shortly before 3 a.m. EST (0800 GMT) on Thursday to pluck the 12-tonne observatory from orbit.
The 45-year-old astrophysicist and astronomer temporarily left a desk job at NASA to rejoin the astronaut corps for this delicate and tricky mission.
Meanwhile, mission commander Ken Bowersox and copilot Scott Horowitz fired manoeuvring jets to keep the shuttle on course and the mission's four spacewalkers checked out their gear.

Astronauts Mark Lee, Steve Smith, Greg Harbaugh and Joe Tanner floated in a jumble of spacesuit parts and toolboxes as they prepared their spacesuits and some of the 300 tools they will use to tinker with the Hubble.
"We're ready to hop in and walk out the door," Lee said on Wednesday in an interview with CBS Radio. "Right now it's looking like we're in real good shape."
The four men are paired into two teams that will work outside on alternate days. The first spacewalk, by Lee and Smith, was scheduled for Thursday night.
Back on earth, controllers at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Centre in Maryland closed the telescope's lens cap in preparation for the shuttle's arrival.
"We're ready for pickup tonight," said Frank Cepollina, the servicing project manager. "Everthing is going great."
The primary goal of this mission is the installation of two new state-of-the-art scientific instruments, each about the size of a large refrigerator -- the first upgrade of the telescope since 1993.

A $105 million multipurpose infrared camera will allow astronomers to see deeper into the universe than ever before and peer through clouds of obscuring dust. A $125 million improved spectrograph will help in the search for massive black holes devouring stars in the centre of galaxies.

"The scientists are all very, very anxious to see these fantastic technology pushes that are in these two instruments," Cepollina said. "If you feel we're getting good science and great imagery now, it's nothing compared to what you are going to see in three or four months from now."
Other planned upgrades included new tape recorders, a more accurate guidance sensor for pointing the telescope and various improved electronic boxes.

The astronauts' work will be complicated by the observatory's fragile set of electricity generating solar arrays. They will get their first look at the 40-foot (12 metre) long wings as the shuttle makes its final approach the telescope on Wednesday night.
"We won't know for sure how delicate they are until we get up there," Lee said.
The Hubble telescope has provided scientists with the first conclusive evidence for the existence of huge black holes and discovery of planetary nurseries around stars.
The telescope has also collected light emission data from distant galaxies and other evidence that the universe may be much younger than previously thought.
Discovery began its 10-day mission with a predawn blastoff from Florida's Kennedy Space Centre early on Tuesday.
